posts.title: Maybe You Don't Need to Climb the Mountain
posts.body:
The Who has been part of my life for as long as I can remember. When I first heard *Tommy* as a pre-teen, I was captivated. I understood the story, but I didn't get its full implications. I certainly didn't imagine that, decades later, after walking my own spiritual path, I would see *Tommy* very differently.

After a traumatic childhood experience, Tommy becomes physically cut off from the world around him. He cannot see, hear or speak. Despite his isolation from others, he becomes a pinball champion and has a devoted following. In a very dramatic sequence, his senses are restored. Enlightenment is achieved through the destruction of his ego. It's powerful. But then something interesting happens.

Other people begin looking to Tommy for answers. And Tommy, believing he has found the way, tries to show them how to reach what he has found by following his path.

It doesn't work.

His followers eventually reject him, and that part of the story resonates with me much differently today. There is a difference between learning from someone and handing them authority over our own journey.

Teachers, healers and spiritual practitioners can introduce us to ideas, challenge us, support us and sometimes help us see something we couldn't see before. But their path is still their path.

I believe the best guides don't ask us to become more like them. They help us become more discerning about what is true for ourselves.

Maybe that's what I finally understand about *Tommy*: nobody can climb the mountain for us. And maybe we don't need to climb it at all.

posts.title: What Life Has Taught Me: The Ego’s Greatest Trick
posts.body:
One of the most profound messages I’ve ever received from my guides was: “Enlightenment is the death of the ego.”

When I first heard those words, I wasn’t entirely sure what they meant. Like many people, I assumed enlightenment was something you achieved. I pictured someone who had reached a higher level of awareness and somehow stood apart from everyone else.

Over the years, that understanding completely changed.

People connect the ego with arrogance but it’s much more subtle than that. The ego wants to be special. It wants to be the most intuitive, the most gifted, or the most enlightened person in the room. It has a way of turning even spirituality into something we can compare, compete over, and use to define ourselves.

I now believe enlightenment asks us to let go of that very need.

The deeper I’ve gone on my own path, the less interested I’ve become in standing out. I don’t need to be the wisest person in the room, and I certainly don’t need people to see me as enlightened. What matters to me now is being present, listening with an open heart, and remembering that every person I meet has something to teach me.

Maybe that’s what my guides meant. Enlightenment doesn’t place us above other people. It reminds us that we were never separate from them in the first place.

posts.title: Something Worth Coming Home To
posts.body:
It took me a while to realize that my own ancestry had a place in my spiritual life. I spent time borrowing from other people’s traditions before turning toward my Italian and Sicilian roots and asking, “What about the people I come from?”

I understand the curiosity about other spiritual paths, including closed practices that require community membership, invitation, or initiation. But while we’re looking elsewhere, we might overlook something meaningful in our own heritage. I believe those traditions can be just as powerful, and even more personally meaningful because they connect us to our ancestors.

Growing up, I watched my grandmother and parents practice Maloik clearing, even though I didn’t understand what they were doing. Maloik is what we call the “evil eye,” traditionally believed to come from another person’s envy or ill wishes. The clearing is a folk ritual intended to release that influence.

At a client’s request, I’m now offering Maloik as part of Reiki sessions. It’s a way of honoring something I witnessed in my own family and bringing that connection into my work.

If you’re curious about your own spiritual roots, start with a family story or a remembered custom. There may be something there you’re ready to understand a little better.
